title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 2: The Formula Sheet
description: A supplier's batch of freshly synthesized compounds needs its paperwork verified — formulas, names, and bonding type — before anything is cleared for the shelf.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Treats a mislabeled formula sheet as a hazard, not a typo.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Can spell the compound names but guesses at the formulas.

formula_sheet.name: Supplier Formula Sheet
formula_sheet.description: Every compound in the batch, listed by name and (allegedly) by formula.

electronegativity_table.name: Electronegativity Table
electronegativity_table.description: Lists each element's electronegativity value for bond-type calculations.

elements.text: New batch from the supplier — a dozen compounds, each with a name and a formula on the sheet. Before any of it goes on the shelf, we verify every formula matches its name.
Can't we just trust the label? They're a supplier, not a mystery.

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the formula sheet.

options.text: "Labels get typo'd all the time — let's verify the charge balance and naming ourselves."

elements.text: Ionic compounds form when a cation and anion combine in whatever ratio makes their total charge zero. Magnesium is 2+, chlorine is 1-, so it takes two chlorides to balance one magnesium: MgCl2.
Ionic compounds also behave a certain way — high melting points, and they conduct electricity once dissolved in water or melted, because the ions are free to move.

config.prompt: Aluminum forms Al3+ ions and oxygen forms O2- ions. What is the correct formula for aluminum oxide? (no spaces, e.g. Al2O3 style)

config.question: Which property is characteristic of ionic compounds like the ones on this sheet?

options.text: High melting point, and conducts electricity when dissolved or molten
Low melting point and never conducts electricity
Exists only as a gas at room temperature
Conducts electricity as a solid but not in solution

config.explanation: The rigid ionic lattice gives ionic compounds high melting points; once the ions are free to move (dissolved or molten), they conduct.

elements.text: A few entries on the sheet are just single elements — O2, N2. Are those compounds too?

No — seven elements naturally exist as diatomic molecules: H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, and I2. They're still pure elements, just bonded to themselves. Molecular compounds are different — two or more nonmetals sharing electrons, like CO2 or H2O.

config.prompt: Sort each entry on the sheet by what it actually is.

config.question: Which of these is NOT one of the seven diatomic elements?
config.explanation: Neon is a noble gas and exists as single, unbonded atoms — it isn't one of the seven diatomic elements (H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2).

elements.text: Whether a bond is ionic or covalent isn't a guess — it comes from the electronegativity difference (delta-EN) between the two atoms. Roughly: under 0.4 is nonpolar covalent, 0.4 to 1.7 is polar covalent, and above 1.7 is ionic.
Sodium (0.9) and chlorine (3.0): delta-EN = 2.1, well past 1.7 — that's ionic, which matches NaCl's behavior.

config.prompt: Nitrogen has an electronegativity of 3.0; hydrogen has 2.1. What is delta-EN for an N-H bond? (one decimal place)

config.question: An N-H bond has delta-EN = 0.9, which falls between 0.4 and 1.7. How should this bond be classified?
config.explanation: 0.4 to 1.7 is the polar covalent range — electrons are shared, but unequally.

elements.text: So how do the names on the sheet actually map to formulas?

Ionic compounds: cation name, then the anion's root plus '-ide' — calcium plus chloride gives CaCl2. Molecular compounds use counting prefixes on both elements: mono-, di-, tri-, tetra- — carbon dioxide is CO2, dinitrogen tetroxide is N2O4.

config.prompt: Calcium forms Ca2+ ions and chlorine forms Cl- ions. What is the correct formula for calcium chloride?

config.question: Using standard covalent-compound prefixes, what is the correct name for N2O4?
config.explanation: Two nitrogens = 'di-nitrogen', four oxygens = 'tetr-oxide' — dinitrogen tetroxide.

elements.text: Every formula, every name, every bond type checks out. This batch is cleared for the shelf.
It's cleared, but a few entries needed a second look. Let's tighten up the naming rules before the next batch.

elements.prompt: The sheet is signed off. What now?

options.text: Show Dev the electronegativity shortcut so he can verify bond types himself next time.
Sign off and shelve the batch. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So the charge tells you the formula, and the electronegativity gap tells you the bond type. Two numbers, and the whole sheet makes sense.

ending.title: Formula Verifier
ending.description: Verified every compound on the sheet from charge balance and electronegativity alone, and taught Dev the shortcut.

ending.title: Batch Signed Off
ending.description: The formula sheet is verified and the batch is shelved. The deeper naming lesson can wait.
